notes:
Account summary
- Prospect evaluating Redwood Dedicated with Burst option as a way to cover predictable spikes without over-reserving GPUs year-round.
- Strong preference for a single vendor for baseline + peaks; wants to avoid stitching together “dedicated baseline + external API spillover”.

Workload / use case
- Primary: customer support agent + summarization pipeline for enterprise customers (mix of online chat + background summarization jobs).
- Secondary: embeddings + reranking for doc-search (“hybrid search” with periodic re-indexing).
- Traffic shape: relatively steady baseline during business hours + sharp spikes during customer launches and weekly batch/backfill jobs.

Peak patterns (as described)
- Baseline: steady inference for chat/summarization (24/7, but much lower overnight).
- Peaks:
  - Weekly indexing/backfill job (Thurs nights): 2–3 hour window, 1.8–2.5x baseline throughput.
  - Launch events: 1–2 days, intermittent 3–5x spikes in request volume; they prefer hard caps + graceful degradation over uncontrolled queuing.
- Quote (paraphrased): “We can plan the spikes; we just don’t want to pay for the peak 30 days a month.”

Dedicated + Burst requirements (must-haves)
- Region pinning: US-only to start (us-east preferred). No cross-region bursting in initial phase acceptable as long as capacity behavior is predictable within region.
- Guardrails:
  - Per-tenant max burst ratio (they asked for at least 2.0x baseline as a purchasable tier; ok if higher tiers require approval).
  - Per-tenant burst cap in absolute units (GPU-seconds or effective tokens/sec) so they can model worst case cost.
  - Cooldown window after extended bursting (they asked if they can configure this vs Redwood defaults; they can live with defaults if documented).
  - Clear denial semantics: immediate denial preferred over “silent latency inflation.” They want explicit 429/overload + reason codes.
  - Deterministic behavior: repeated requests under same conditions shouldn’t oscillate between admitted/denied due to telemetry jitter.
- Fairness / noisy neighbor protection:
  - They specifically asked how Redwood prevents one tenant from starving others in a shared burst pool.
  - Want reassurance that non-burst tenants’ SLOs are protected and that there is a global fleet safety cap / circuit breaker.
- Observability:
  - Customer-visible view of: burst usage vs cap, burst request admit/deny counts, top denial reasons, and latency deltas during burst windows.
  - Needs exportable report for their Finance team (monthly burst usage summary) and for internal incident reviews.

Performance targets (current ask)
- Online chat: p95 end-to-end model latency target < 300ms for typical prompts (they acknowledged this is model/seq dependent; they care most about regression during neighbor bursts).
- Background batch: throughput-oriented; they will accept queuing/backpressure as long as it’s explicit and cost-predictable.

Security / compliance requirements
- SSO/SAML for Console and role-based access for who can enable/modify burst settings.
- Audit logging: must include burst enable/disable, limit changes, and any admin override actions; wants retention controls and export path.
- KMS: customer-managed keys preferred (or at minimum documented key management + encryption at rest/in transit).

Open questions from EmberStack
- Is burst capacity “guaranteed” in any form, or strictly best-effort subject to admission? They want language they can pass to their own customers.
- What happens when cap is hit: 429 vs queue? They prefer 429 + reason code + retry-after guidance.
- How is billing metered for burst: GPU-seconds vs token-based? Need a clear line item and reconciliation story.

Internal Redwood notes / next steps
- Stephanie to send: burst option one-pager + draft pricing bands + written explanation of denial reason codes and recommended client retry strategy.
- Markus to schedule: 60-min architecture/security follow-up w/ their platform lead (focus: audit events + VPC/private connectivity options + dashboards).
- Loop in Legal (Michael Grant) for order form addendum language: define burst, disclaimers around pool admission, and SLO scope.

Deal risk
- If we can’t provide crisp, customer-consumable docs around guardrails/denials and audit events, they may default to over-provisioning (competitor dedicated) or multi-vendor spillover.
